section.title: Sarah's Burial
section.sectionRationale: Sarah dies, and Abraham buys a field and a cave to bury her. It reads like a legal deed, yet it is quietly momentous: the sojourner who was promised the whole land now owns his first small plot of it, a burial ground held in hope of resurrection.
section.thesis: In grief Abraham insists on paying full price for a burial site, and the man who owns nothing gains his first foothold in the promised land, a down payment of the inheritance held by faith beyond death.
section.frameNote: Four scenes: Sarah's death and mourning; Abraham's request for a burial site; the careful purchase of Machpelah; the field secured as his possession.

verses.text: Now Sarah lived to be 127 years old.
She died in Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) in the land of Canaan, and Abraham went out to mourn and to weep for her.

units.label: Abraham asks for a burial site

verses.text: Then Abraham got up from beside his dead wife and said to the Hittites,
“I am a {{ger|foreigner and an outsider}} among you. Give me a burial site among you so that I can bury my dead.”
The Hittites replied to Abraham,
“Listen to us, sir. You are God’s chosen one among us. Bury your dead in the finest of our tombs. None of us will withhold his tomb for burying your dead.”
Then Abraham rose and bowed down before the people of the land, the Hittites.
“If you are willing for me to bury my dead,” he said to them, “listen to me, and approach Ephron son of Zohar on my behalf
to sell me the {{machpelah|cave of Machpelah}} that belongs to him; it is at the end of his field. Let him sell it to me in your presence for full price, so that I may have a burial site.”
Now Ephron was sitting among the sons of Heth. So in the presence of all the Hittites who had come to the gate of his city, Ephron the Hittite answered Abraham,
“No, my lord. Listen to me. I give you the field, and I give you the cave that is in it. I give it to you in the presence of my people. Bury your dead.”
Again Abraham bowed down before the people of the land
and said to Ephron in their presence, “If you will please listen to me, I will pay you the price of the field. Accept it from me, so that I may bury my dead there.”
Ephron answered Abraham,
“Listen to me, my lord. The land is worth four hundred shekels of silver, but what is that between you and me? Bury your dead.”
Abraham agreed to Ephron’s terms and weighed out for him the price he had named in the hearing of the Hittites: four hundred shekels of silver, according to the standard of the merchants.

units.label: The field secured as a possession
units.note: a foothold in the promised land

verses.text: So Ephron’s field at Machpelah near Mamre, the cave that was in it, and all the trees within the boundaries of the field were deeded over
to Abraham’s {{achuzzah|possession}} in the presence of all the Hittites who had come to the gate of his city.
After this, Abraham buried his wife Sarah in the cave of the field at Machpelah near Mamre (that is, Hebron) in the land of Canaan.
So the field and its cave were deeded by the Hittites to Abraham as a burial site.

ger.gloss: A resident foreigner, a sojourner who lives among a people without full rights of citizenship or landholding. Abraham calls himself a ger to explain why he must ask to buy ground. The word captures the whole patriarchal life, dwelling in the land of promise as strangers who own none of it yet.

machpelah.gloss: A place name for the field and cave near Hebron that Abraham buys, likely meaning double or the doubled cave. It becomes the ancestral tomb of the patriarchs, where Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob, and Leah are buried, Israel's first and abiding claim on the land.

achuzzah.gloss: A holding, property, or possession, from a root meaning to grasp or take hold. It is the formal legal term for owned land. That the promised land first becomes Abraham's achuzzah as a grave is deeply poignant, a foothold of inheritance secured even in the face of death.

basic.context: Sarah, Abraham's wife and the mother of the promised son, dies at 127. Abraham mourns, then negotiates carefully with the local Hittites to buy a cave and field as a burial place. He refuses to take it as a gift and pays full price. The key question is why the writer devotes a whole chapter to a real estate transaction.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a historical account, and its slow, legal detail is the point. Abraham, promised the whole land, secures his first tiny plot of it, and he does so as a lawful, honoured purchase before witnesses. The question is what this small deed says about faith in God's promise in the face of death.
basic.originalLanguages: Abraham calls himself a ger, a resident foreigner with no land rights, which is why he must buy ground. He purchases the cave of Machpelah, and it becomes his achuzzah, his legal possession or holding. That the promised land is first held as a grave gives the ordinary words a weight of hope.
basic.typology: The burial ground held in a land not yet possessed is a picture of the whole life of faith, which holds God's promises even through death. The cave where the dead are laid in hope anticipates the tomb that could not hold Christ, and the resurrection life His people await.
basic.christ: Abraham buries Sarah trusting God beyond the grave, the same hope fulfilled when Christ rose from a borrowed tomb. The down payment of the land points to the inheritance secured for believers, and to the day the whole earth is given to the meek in the risen Lord.
basic.god: God is faithful to His promise even when its fulfilment seems distant and death intervenes. He gives Abraham a real, if small, foothold in the land, a token that His word will not fail. He is the God of the living, in whom the buried are held in hope.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 11 says the patriarchs died in faith, not having received the promises, but seeing them from afar. Acts 7 recalls this burial plot. Genesis 49 and 50 return to Machpelah as the patriarchs' tomb.
basic.oneStory: The sojourner gains his first plot of the promised land, a grave, held in hope that God keeps His word beyond death. It is a quiet pledge of the full inheritance, secured at last in the risen Christ who opens the tomb.

context.literary:
Genesis 23 is framed by a matching pair of place notes. Sarah dies 'in Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) in the land of Canaan,' verse 2, and she is buried 'at Machpelah near Mamre (that is, Hebron) in the land of Canaan,' verse 19. Between those two lines the chapter moves from a death to a deed, and the phrase 'in the land of Canaan' at both ends quietly names what is really at stake.

The middle of the chapter is a negotiation in three rounds, and each round has the same shape: Abraham speaks, the other party answers with a courteous offer, and Abraham presses again. First he addresses the Hittites as a body, verses 3 to 6. Then he bows and asks them to approach Ephron, verses 7 to 9. Finally Ephron himself speaks, first offering a gift, verse 11, then naming a price, verse 15, and Abraham weighs out the silver, verse 16. Abraham bows twice, verses 7 and 12, and each bow comes just before he refuses a kindness he cannot accept.

The narrator builds the scene out of repeated words. 'Listen' runs through nearly every speech, verses 6, 8, 11, 13 and 15, until the deal is finally struck 'in the hearing of the Hittites,' verse 16. The phrase 'bury my dead' or 'bury your dead' comes again and again, so that grief is never far beneath the business. And the witnesses are named at every turn: 'in your presence,' 'in the presence of my people,' 'in the presence of all the Hittites who had come to the gate of his city,' verses 9, 11 and 18. The legal atmosphere is not decoration. It is the point.

The chapter's placement matters too. It follows the news of Nahor's family, Genesis 22:20-24, which quietly introduces Rebekah just before Sarah leaves the story. It begins the last movement of Abraham's life, three scenes that tie up his affairs: a grave for Sarah, Genesis 23, a wife for Isaac, Genesis 24, and his own death and burial in this same cave, Genesis 25:9-10.
context.historical:
Hebron lies in the hill country south of Jerusalem, and it was an old city. Numbers 13:22 notes that it was built seven years before Zoan in Egypt, and Joshua 14:15 explains the older name: Kiriath-arba was named after Arba, 'the greatest man among the Anakim.' Abraham had pitched his tents near Mamre by Hebron long before this, Genesis 13:18, but Genesis 22:19 last left him living at Beersheba, which may be why the text says he 'went' to mourn for Sarah.

The people Abraham deals with are the 'sons of Heth,' as the BSB footnote on verse 3 notes, descendants of Canaan's son Heth in the Table of Nations, Genesis 10:15. How they relate to the great Hittite kingdom of Anatolia is uncertain; Genesis presents them as a local people settled in Hebron, with their own city gate and council.

The gate was where public business was done, as it still was in Boaz's day, when he bought Elimelech's land with 'the elders and all the people at the gate' as his witnesses, Ruth 4:9-11. A sale made there, before everyone who 'had come to the gate of his city,' could not later be denied. Money was not yet coined. Silver was weighed, and 'the standard of the merchants,' verse 16, points to weights that traders would accept. Four hundred shekels, which the BSB footnote puts at about 4.6 kilograms, was a large sum. Jeremiah paid seventeen shekels for a field, Jeremiah 32:9, and David paid fifty shekels for Araunah's threshing floor and oxen, 2 Samuel 24:24.

As a ger, a resident alien, Abraham had no inherited right to land. The Hittites' first offer, the use of 'the finest of our tombs,' verse 6, would have been generous but would have left Sarah lying in a Hittite family grave on Hittite sufferance. The listing of the field, the cave and 'all the trees within the boundaries,' verse 17, reads like the precise language of a property record.
context.canonical:
Machpelah becomes the family grave of the patriarchs. Abraham is laid there beside Sarah, Genesis 25:9-10. Jacob later lists all who rest there, 'Abraham and his wife Sarah... Isaac and his wife Rebekah... and there I buried Leah,' Genesis 49:31, and asks to be buried there himself, which Joseph carries out, Genesis 50:13. Rachel, by contrast, is buried on the way to Bethlehem, Genesis 35:19. Jacob's insistence, 'Do not bury me in Egypt,' Genesis 47:29, and Joseph's command about his bones, Genesis 50:25 and Exodus 13:19, all grow from this chapter. A patriarch's grave in Canaan was a claim on the future.

Hebron itself goes on to matter. Caleb receives it as his inheritance because he 'wholly followed the LORD,' Joshua 14:13-14. David is anointed king there, first over Judah and then over all Israel, 2 Samuel 2:1-4 and 5:3-5. The town where Abraham could only buy a grave becomes the first capital of the promised king.

The language of Abraham's self description echoes through Scripture. Leviticus 25:23 tells Israel, even after the conquest, 'you are but foreigners and residents with Me.' David prays, 'we are foreigners and strangers in Your presence, as were all our forefathers,' 1 Chronicles 29:15, and Psalm 39:12 says the same.

In the New Testament Stephen notes that God gave Abraham 'no inheritance here, not even a foot of ground,' Acts 7:5, and later speaks of a tomb 'that Abraham had bought,' Acts 7:16, compressing this purchase with Jacob's at Shechem, Genesis 33:19. Hebrews 11:9-16 reads the patriarchs' whole life in the land as faith that looked for 'a better country, a heavenly one,' and 1 Peter 2:11 calls the church 'foreigners and exiles.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wrote for a people who were themselves on the way to a land they did not yet hold. For Israel in the wilderness, or in the land afterward, this chapter was a title deed. It showed that their fathers' claim to Canaan was not only a promise spoken in private visions but was also anchored in a public, witnessed, paid for piece of ground, and that the graves of Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, Leah and Jacob lay in it. The land they entered already held their ancestors' bones.

The author also meant Israel to learn how faith behaves when God's promises are slow. Abraham does not seize land by force, nor does he accept a favour that would bind him to the Canaanites, as earlier he refused to be made rich by the king of Sodom, Genesis 14:23. He pays in full, openly, and with courtesy. Faith trusts God for the whole while dealing honestly for the part.

Finally, the chapter teaches that faith grieves. Abraham 'went out to mourn and to weep for her,' verse 2, before he 'got up from beside his dead wife,' verse 3. The man of faith is not above tears. He weeps, and then he rises to act on the promise.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes one purchase in one culture; it does not lay down how believers must bury their dead or conduct business. Its bargaining customs, the weighing of silver and the council at the gate belong to their time.

What carries over is a pattern of conduct and hope. Believers are to deal openly and fairly with neighbours outside the covenant, as Abraham does, bowing to them with real respect even while declining their gift. Grief is right and good; Paul does not forbid it but says believers need not 'grieve like the rest, who are without hope,' 1 Thessalonians 4:13.

Many Christians have drawn from the patriarchs' care for their dead a reverence for the body and a preference for burial as a witness to resurrection hope. The chapter shows that care, but it does not command a method. Its lasting call is to live as foreigners and exiles who still act on God's promise, 1 Peter 2:11.

debates.question: Why does Abraham insist on paying full price when the field is offered to him freely?

views.label: To secure a title no one can revoke
views.case: A gift in the ancient world could create obligations or be disputed by heirs. A purchase for 'full price,' verse 9, made before every witness at the gate, verse 18, gave Abraham an achuzzah, a permanent holding, that no later generation of Hittites could reclaim.

views.label: To act on faith in the promise
views.case: God had promised the whole land to Abraham's offspring, Genesis 17:8. Buying a grave in it, rather than borrowing a Hittite tomb or carrying Sarah back to Haran, is a deliberate act of hope. The burial ground is a statement that his family's future lies here.

views.label: To keep himself free of debt to the Canaanites
views.case: Abraham had already refused to let the king of Sodom say, 'I have made Abram rich,' Genesis 14:23. Accepting the land as a gift would place him in Ephron's debt. Paying keeps the promised inheritance a gift from God alone.

debates.bearing: The three readings work together. Legal prudence, faith and integrity combine, so that the first parcel of the promised land is held by right, in hope, and owed to no one but God.

debates.question: Is Ephron being generous or shrewd?

views.label: Genuine courtesy
views.case: Ephron speaks warmly, 'I give you the field... Bury your dead,' verse 11, and the Hittites honour Abraham as 'God's chosen one among us,' verse 6. On this reading the offer is sincere and Abraham's refusal is his own choice.

views.label: Polite bargaining toward a high price
views.case: Many readers hear the conventions of the marketplace. Ephron offers the whole field when Abraham asked only for the cave at 'the end of his field,' verse 9, then names a steep price while calling it a trifle, 'what is that between you and me?' verse 15. The price compares with seventeen shekels for Jeremiah's field, Jeremiah 32:9.

views.label: Passing on the burdens of ownership
views.case: Some have suggested that selling the whole field, rather than a cave on its edge, transferred to Abraham whatever duties went with the land. The theory was once linked to Hittite law, but the parallels are debated and cannot be pressed.

debates.bearing: The text does not judge Ephron, and it does not need to. Its focus is on Abraham, who neither haggles nor complains but weighs out exactly what was asked, so that the transaction cannot later be questioned.

debates.question: How does Stephen's reference to 'the tomb that Abraham had bought' in Acts 7:16 relate to this chapter?

views.label: A deliberate compression
views.case: Stephen's speech moves fast through centuries, and he joins two purchases, Abraham's cave at Hebron, Genesis 23, and Jacob's plot at Shechem, Genesis 33:19 and Joshua 24:32, into one sentence about the patriarchs' burial. Speakers of his day often summarised in this way.

views.label: An accurate record of Stephen's words
views.case: Others note that Luke faithfully reports what Stephen said in a charged setting, and the compression belongs to the speech rather than to Luke's own narrative.

views.label: An otherwise unrecorded purchase
views.case: Some older interpreters suggested Abraham also bought ground at Shechem, where he had built an altar, Genesis 12:6-7, though Genesis does not say so.

debates.bearing: Whatever the solution, Stephen's point is clear and matches Genesis 23. The patriarchs owned no inheritance to live on, only graves, and those graves were held in hope of what God had promised, Acts 7:5.

study.originalLanguages:
Abraham's self description in verse 4 is a pair, ger ve toshav, 'a foreigner and an outsider.' The ger is a resident alien, someone who lives among a people without belonging to their land by birth. The toshav is a settler or temporary resident, from the verb yashav, to sit or dwell. Together they make a standard phrase for someone who lives in a place but holds no inheritance there. The same pair returns when God tells Israel, 'you are but foreigners and residents with Me,' Leviticus 25:23, and when David and the psalmist confess, 1 Chronicles 29:15 and Psalm 39:12. The Greek Septuagint rendered Abraham's phrase with paroikos and parepidemos, and 1 Peter 2:11 uses that same pair when it calls believers 'foreigners and exiles.' Peter is putting the church in Abraham's sandals at the grave of Sarah.

The word ger comes from the verb gur, to sojourn, and Genesis keeps using it for the patriarchs' life. God promised Abraham 'the land where you are residing,' Genesis 17:8, literally the land of your sojournings, and the same expression recurs for Isaac and Jacob, Genesis 28:4, 36:7 and 37:1, and Exodus 6:4. The land of promise is, for now, the land of sojourning.

The 'possession' Abraham seeks is achuzzah, a noun from the verb achaz, to grasp or take hold. In verse 4 he asks literally for 'a possession of a grave,' and the same phrase closes the chapter, verse 20, translated 'burial site.' This is the word of Genesis 17:8, where God promised all Canaan 'as an eternal possession,' and it returns in Genesis 48:4. In Leviticus 25 it becomes the technical term for family land, the holding each clan returns to in the Jubilee, Leviticus 25:10. Abraham's first achuzzah is a grave.

The Hittites call Abraham nesi Elohim, verse 6. Nasi is the word for a prince or leader, the same word later used for Ishmael's twelve princes, Genesis 25:16. Joined to Elohim it can mean 'a prince of God' or, as a superlative, 'a mighty prince'; the BSB's 'God's chosen one' leans toward the first. Either way the sojourner is honoured as someone great.

Two small words carry the legal weight. Abraham asks to buy the cave 'for full price,' verse 9, literally 'for full silver,' the same phrase David uses when he insists on paying Ornan for the threshing floor, 1 Chronicles 21:22 and 21:24. And the verb for the field being 'deeded over,' verses 17 and 20, is qum, to rise or stand, the same verb used when Abraham 'got up' from beside Sarah, verse 3, and 'rose' to bow, verse 7. Abraham rises from his dead, and the field 'stands' as his. A sale that stands is one that holds good.

The name Machpelah itself seems related to a root meaning to double or fold, and the Septuagint rendered it 'the double cave,' though the exact sense is uncertain.

typology.type: The purchased grave as a first instalment of the land
typology.fulfillment: The cave is a real piece of Canaan, legally Abraham's, yet only a fraction of what God swore. It functions as a pledge that the rest will follow. Paul uses that idea for the Holy Spirit, 'the pledge of our inheritance until the redemption of those who are God's possession,' Ephesians 1:14, and 2 Corinthians 1:22. The escalation is great: Abraham's pledge was a field for the dead, while the believer's pledge is the living Spirit of God within. The type falls short because a cave could be lost or forgotten, while the Spirit seals the heir for the day of redemption, Ephesians 1:13.

typology.type: The tomb held in hope of resurrection
typology.fulfillment: Sarah is laid in a tomb in the land of promise, and generations of patriarchs follow her there, each one waiting. Christ was also laid in a tomb, a new one in a garden, John 19:41, but His tomb was not a waiting room. He rose as 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20, and the women found the stone rolled away, Luke 24:2-3. The correspondence is a grave held in hope; the escalation is that Christ's grave is empty, and so the graves of all who are His, Machpelah included, will be emptied too, 1 Thessalonians 4:14.

Abraham lives in the promised land without owning it, 'a foreigner and an outsider,' verse 4. Hebrews 11:13 gathers the patriarchs under that description, 'strangers and exiles on the earth,' and 1 Peter 2:11 applies the same words to the church. Christ Himself had 'no place to lay His head,' Luke 9:58, and was buried in a tomb that belonged to another man, Matthew 27:60. The escalation is that the true Heir took the stranger's place, so that strangers might become 'fellow citizens with the saints,' Ephesians 2:19. The type falls short because Abraham's sojourn ended in a grave, while ours ends in a city God has prepared, Hebrews 11:16.

typology.type: The full price weighed out for a possession
typology.fulfillment: Abraham will not take the field as a gift; he pays the whole price publicly so that it is truly his. The New Testament speaks of God's people as a possession bought at a price, 'you were bought at a price,' 1 Corinthians 6:20, a church 'which He purchased with His own blood,' Acts 20:28. This is an echo rather than a declared type, and it breaks at the key point: Abraham paid silver for ground, while believers were redeemed 'not with perishable things such as silver or gold,' but 'with the precious blood of Christ,' 1 Peter 1:18-19.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first by the promise it keeps alive. Abraham buys a grave because he believes God's word, 'To your offspring I will give this land,' Genesis 12:7. Paul reads that promise as larger than Canaan: Abraham and his offspring would be 'heir of the world,' Romans 4:13, and the offspring is finally 'One, who is Christ,' Galatians 3:16. Jesus Himself says the meek 'will inherit the earth,' Matthew 5:5. The one cave at Machpelah is the first square of a map that Christ will fill.

It leads to Christ by the pattern of a grave held in hope. The patriarchs are buried in the land they were promised, waiting. Jesus answers the question that hangs over their tomb when He argues from the words 'I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.' 'He is not the God of the dead, but of the living,' Matthew 22:32, and Luke adds, 'for to Him all are alive,' Luke 20:38. The people in Machpelah are not lost to God. They wait for the resurrection that Jesus announces, 'I am the resurrection and the life,' John 11:25.

It leads to Christ by a striking contrast between two purchases of burial ground. Abraham weighs out honest silver for a family tomb. At the end of the Gospels the chief priests take thirty pieces of silver, Judas's blood money, and 'used the money to buy the potter's field as a burial place for foreigners,' Matthew 27:7. The price of Christ's betrayal buys a grave for strangers. What Abraham could only do for his own household, Christ's death opens for outsiders, so that those 'far away have been brought near through the blood of Christ,' Ephesians 2:13.

It leads to Christ in the tomb itself. Jesus, like Sarah, was buried in a tomb that another had provided, Matthew 27:59-60, cut in rock in a garden, John 19:41. But where Machpelah received body after body over generations, that tomb was found empty on the third day, Luke 24:3. Christ is 'the firstfruits,' 1 Corinthians 15:20, the first of a harvest that includes Abraham and Sarah.

A note of care keeps this reading honest. The New Testament never says that Machpelah is a figure of Christ's tomb, and the cave, the trees and the silver are not coded messages. The link rests on the promise the chapter acts on and on Jesus' own use of 'the God of Abraham.' Hebrews states the conclusion plainly: these all 'died in faith, without having received the things they were promised,' Hebrews 11:13, and 'together with us they would be made perfect,' Hebrews 11:40. That perfecting is Christ's work.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God whose promises move slowly and surely. Abraham has lived in Canaan for more than sixty years by this point, and all he owns of it is what he now pays for. God had said as much, warning that the land would come to Abraham's descendants only 'in the fourth generation,' Genesis 15:16, while Abraham himself would 'go to your fathers in peace,' Genesis 15:15. God is not late. He keeps His own timetable and tells His people what it is.

God is also the unseen actor in a chapter where He never speaks. There is no vision, no angel and no word from heaven. Yet the Hittites, of all people, call Abraham 'God's chosen one among us,' verse 6, echoing what Abimelech had said earlier, 'God is with you in all that you do,' Genesis 21:22. God's blessing on Abraham is visible even to outsiders, and it opens the door for a lawful purchase that might easily have been refused.

The chapter shows God's faithfulness through death rather than around it. Sarah was the woman through whom the promise came, the woman of whom God asked, 'Is anything too difficult for the LORD?' Genesis 18:14. Now she dies, and nothing in the chapter pretends otherwise. Yet the promise does not die with her, because it never rested on her strength. God is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, 'not the God of the dead, but of the living,' Matthew 22:32. Those who die in His promise are still held by it.

God also shows His ownership of the land. Leviticus 25:23 later explains why even Israel could never sell land permanently: 'it is Mine, and you are but foreigners and residents with Me.' Abraham's title to his little field is real and legal, yet beneath it lies a deeper title. The whole earth is the Lord's, and He gives it as He chooses.

For worship, the chapter invites a quiet trust. God's people may weep at a graveside and still be certain. They may hold only a little of what God has promised and still act as though the rest is coming. Hebrews says that because the patriarchs lived and died this way, 'God is not ashamed to be called their God, for He has prepared a city for them,' Hebrews 11:16.

crossReferences.note: God promised Abraham 'all the land of Canaan' as 'an eternal possession,' using the same word achuzzah that describes the burial site in Genesis 23:4 and 23:20. The first eternal possession Abraham actually holds is a grave, bought with silver, a small pledge of the whole.

God had told Abraham that his descendants would be strangers in another land and would return only 'in the fourth generation,' while Abraham himself would die in peace. Genesis 23 is that word coming true in part. Abraham owns only a grave, exactly as God had forewarned.

On his deathbed in Egypt Jacob lists everyone buried at Machpelah and insists on joining them. The field Abraham bought for Sarah has become the family's claim on Canaan, so that even from Egypt the patriarchs look back to this plot as home.

God tells Israel that the land 'must not be sold permanently, because it is Mine, and you are but foreigners and residents with Me.' The phrase repeats Abraham's self description in Genesis 23:4. Even when Israel owns the land, it lives there as God's guest.

On the eve of exile Jeremiah buys a field, weighs out silver, signs the deed before witnesses and stores it 'for a long time,' because 'fields... will again be bought in this land.' Like Abraham, he makes a lawful purchase in the land as an act of faith in God's promise.

Stephen says God gave Abraham 'no inheritance here, not even a foot of ground,' yet promised it to him and his descendants. A grave is not an inheritance to live on, so Genesis 23 confirms Stephen's point: Abraham held the promise, not the land.

The patriarchs 'died in faith, without having received the things they were promised,' confessing that they were 'strangers and exiles.' Abraham's words at Sarah's grave are exactly that confession, and Hebrews says it shows they were 'seeking a country of their own,' a better one.

Peter calls the church 'foreigners and exiles,' using the same Greek pair the Septuagint used for Abraham's words in Genesis 23:4. Believers are to live as Abraham did in Hebron, honourable among their neighbours while holding their true inheritance in hope.

Jesus argues for the resurrection from God's title, 'the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.' Those three men and their wives lay in Machpelah. Jesus insists that God is still their God, so the grave Abraham bought is not the end of their story.

The chief priests use Judas's thirty pieces of silver to buy 'the potter's field as a burial place for foreigners.' It is a dark mirror of Genesis 23: silver weighed out for burial ground, but here the price of the Saviour's betrayal buys a grave for strangers.

Christ 'has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.' The patriarchs in Machpelah are among those who have fallen asleep, and Christ's rising is the pledge that their graves, like His, will not keep their dead.

The Spirit is 'the pledge of our inheritance until the redemption of those who are God's possession.' Abraham's cave was a first instalment of the land; the Spirit is the believer's first instalment of the new creation, a far greater pledge of a far greater inheritance.

study.oneStory:
In the beginning God gave humanity the whole earth to fill and rule, Genesis 1:28, and in the fall He sentenced the man to return to the ground, 'for dust you are, and to dust you shall return,' Genesis 3:19. Genesis 23 stands at the meeting point of those two words. The man to whom God promised a land now asks for a piece of ground to lay his dead in. The promise of the earth and the curse of death meet in a cave at Hebron.

The chapter answers the promise to Abraham. God had called him to a land He would show him, Genesis 12:1, and sworn to give it to his offspring, Genesis 12:7 and 17:8. Sixty years later Abraham still lives in tents. The purchase at Machpelah is the first sign that the promise is more than words. It also sets up what follows. Every patriarch will be carried back to this grave, and Jacob's and Joseph's instructions about their bones, Genesis 47:29-30 and 50:25, keep Israel's eyes on Canaan through four hundred years in Egypt. When Israel finally enters the land, it enters a country where its fathers already lie buried.

Yet even the conquest does not finish the story. Israel is told it remains a guest on God's land, Leviticus 25:23, and later loses the land in exile. The prophets then speak of a deeper hope: 'Your dead will live; their bodies will rise,' Isaiah 26:19, and 'many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake,' Daniel 12:2.

That hope comes to rest in Christ. He was buried in a garden tomb and rose, the firstfruits of the dead, 1 Corinthians 15:20. In Him believers are Abraham's offspring and 'heirs according to the promise,' Galatians 3:29, and they receive the Spirit as the pledge of their inheritance, Ephesians 1:14. They still live as foreigners and exiles, 1 Peter 2:11, and they still bury their dead in hope.

The new creation brings the story home. Death and mourning are gone, Revelation 21:4, and the meek inherit the earth, Matthew 5:5. The man who owned only a grave will own a world, and Sarah, who was laid in a cave at Hebron, will rise to see the city God prepared for those who died in faith, Hebrews 11:16.

quiz.q: Why did Abraham need to ask the Hittites for a burial site?

options.text: Because he was a resident foreigner who owned no land in Canaan.
options.note: Abraham calls himself a ger, a sojourner without land rights, in verse 4.

options.text: Because he had not yet settled anywhere in the region.
options.note: He does live in the land, but the real issue is that as a foreigner he owns none of it.

options.text: Because the Hittites had driven him from his own land.
options.note: The Hittites honour him; there is no expulsion in the account.

options.text: Because God had told him not to buy land.
options.note: There is no such command; Abraham freely negotiates to buy the field.

quiz.q: How did Abraham respond to Ephron's offer to give him the field for free?

options.text: He insisted on paying the full price and weighed out the silver.
options.note: Abraham refuses a gift and pays four hundred shekels before witnesses.

options.text: He accepted the field but gave gifts in return.
options.note: He does not accept it as a gift at all; he pays the stated price in full.

options.text: He took the field freely as an honour due to him.
options.note: The opposite; Abraham declines the free offer and insists on buying it.

options.text: He refused the field and buried Sarah elsewhere.
options.note: He buys Machpelah and buries Sarah there.

quiz.q: What is significant about the field of Machpelah becoming Abraham's possession?

options.text: It is his first permanent holding in the promised land, a foothold of the inheritance.
options.note: The land God promised is first held by Abraham as his own deeded achuzzah.

options.text: It shows Abraham had grown wealthy enough to buy land.
options.note: His wealth is real, but the deeper point is the foothold in the promised land.

options.text: It proves the Hittites had surrendered all their territory.
options.note: Abraham buys only one field; the Hittites keep their land.

options.text: It means Abraham had given up hope in God's promise.
options.note: The purchase is an act of hope in the promise, not a giving up of it.

quiz.q: How does this burial account connect to resurrection hope?

options.text: Abraham buries Sarah in the promised land trusting God beyond death, a hope fulfilled in the risen Christ.
options.note: The grave held in hope points to the tomb that could not hold Jesus.

options.text: It teaches that faithful people avoid grief at death.
options.note: Abraham genuinely mourns; the hope does not remove grief but holds through it.

options.text: It shows that the dead simply cease to exist.
options.note: The patriarchs are buried in hope; Jesus calls God the God of the living.

options.text: It proves that the promised land was only ever symbolic.
options.note: The land and the deed are real; they anchor a real inheritance and hope.

quiz.q: What does Abraham's careful, honest purchase reveal about him?

options.text: He deals with integrity before witnesses and stakes a real claim on God's promise.
options.note: Honest dealing and faith in the promise meet in the public, full price purchase.

options.text: He was mainly concerned to appear respectable to the Hittites.
options.note: He is honourable, but the driving motive is a lawful, hope filled claim on the land, not mere appearance.

options.text: He was reluctant to spend money on a burial.
options.note: He willingly pays a large sum; cost is not his hesitation.

options.text: He distrusted God and sought security in property.
options.note: The purchase expresses faith in God's promise, not distrust of it.

questions: Abraham mourned and wept for Sarah, and Scripture does not rush him past it. How does it help to know that honest grief and steady faith can live together?
Abraham held on to God's promise even as he buried the one he loved. What promise of God do you need to hold on to in a season of loss?
The land was first possessed as a grave, a foothold of a much larger inheritance. Where are you being asked to trust God for a fulfilment you can only glimpse now?
Abraham dealt honestly and openly, paying full price before witnesses. Where is God calling you to integrity even when a shortcut is offered?
The buried patriarchs rest in hope of resurrection. How does the empty tomb of Christ change the way you face death, your own and others'?

translationNotes.note: Kiriath-arba is identified as Hebron; the parenthesis preserves both the older name and the later, familiar one.
Four hundred shekels of silver was a substantial sum, weighed out according to the merchants' standard, marking a full and honest price rather than a bargain.
